evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.3.132: Apronium spōnsiōne lacessīvit (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 94: tē spōnsiōne prōvocō, I bet you
terms.comment: In Roman law a wager on the outcome of a case, the loser to pay a sum (Lewis & Short); of betting in general from Juvenal on. To bet someone, aliquem spōnsiōne prōvocāre or lacessere; to win a bet, spōnsiōne vincere (Cic. Quinct. 84). Its first sense is a solemn promise, a guarantee (see guarantee).
A pledge or security (Lewis & Short); in Vergil’s singing match, the stake: pignore certāre, to compete for a stake, to bet.

evidence: Verg. Ecl. 3.31–32: Ego hanc vitulam … dēpōnō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Its usual sense is to lay down, put aside, deposit (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Traupman 93: I bet he has taken off, pōnō eum abīsse
terms.comment: Pōnō is “I take it, I lay it down as given” (pōnō satis in eō fuisse ōrātiōnis, Cic. Brut. 165; see assume): a premise, not a wager. To bet someone, spōnsiōne prōvocāre (above).

phrases.latin: tū dīc mēcum quō pignore certēs
phrases.english: you tell me what you will stake against me

phrases.latin: Tē spōnsiōne prōvocō illum nōn esse victūrum.
phrases.english: I bet you he won’t win.

sources: Lewis & Short: sponsio · Lewis & Short: pignus · Lewis & Short: depono
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 94 (bet).
Quotation from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-ranieri-eclogae, after Luke Ranieri, The Conversational Latin of Virgil’s Eclogues, 2024).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
